descriptor.note: Copied by a script from the Victorian Curriculum Version 2.0 on 15 November 2026, not typed from memory.
descriptor.text: sound can make materials vibrate and vibrating materials can make sound; different actions can be used to produce sounds of varying pitch and volume
descriptor.attribution: Victorian Curriculum Foundation to Level 10 content is © VCAA, licensed CC BY-NC 3.0 Australia. The official curriculum is on the VCAA website.

paraphrase.note: My reading of the description and its achievement standard. The achievement standard wording was checked in the curriculum: students describe the effect of sound energy on objects and demonstrate how different sounds can be produced.
paraphrase.text: Sound and vibration go both ways. When something vibrates (shakes back and forth very fast) it makes a sound, and a sound can make other things vibrate. Students also need to make sounds on purpose: louder or quieter, higher or lower, by changing what they do or what they do it to. The assessable skills are describing what a sound does to an object and showing how to produce different sounds.
asks_for: Vibrating materials make sound. Every sound has something vibrating behind it, even when the vibration is too small or too fast to see.
Sound can make materials vibrate, such as rice jumping on a drum skin when someone claps nearby.
Different actions (striking, plucking, blowing, scraping, shaking) produce different sounds.
Sounds vary in volume (loud or quiet) and in pitch (high or low), and these are two different things.
not_asking: How sound travels from the source to the ear, or what it travels through. The description stops at making sounds and what sound does to materials, although two elaborations touch on echoes and on earmuffs.
Sound as a wave, with frequency and amplitude. That is Levels 9 and 10 (VC2S10U14).
The parts of the ear and how hearing works.
Measuring sound in decibels or pitch in hertz. Informal comparisons (louder, quieter, higher, lower) are enough.

key_questions.note: The question and its content are my judgement. The twanged ruler, tuning forks and speaking are examples in a VCAA elaboration. The point about less obvious sounds comes from the research summaries.
key_questions.question: What is happening when something makes a sound?
know: To vibrate is to shake back and forth very quickly.
When a sound is made, something is vibrating: a string, a ruler, a drum skin, the air in a whistle, the voice box in your throat.
When the vibrating stops, the sound stops.
understand: All sounds come from vibrations, including sounds where nothing can be seen moving, such as a clap, a bang or a voice.
do: Find what is vibrating for a range of sounds by looking, touching and listening.
Stop a sound by stopping the vibration, for example by holding a ringing triangle or a twanging ruler.

key_questions.note: My judgement. This is the first half of the description and the first half of the achievement standard sentence (the effect of sound energy on objects). A VCAA elaboration has students investigate how sound energy makes things vibrate.
key_questions.question: What can a sound do to the things around it?
know: A sound can make other things vibrate.
A loud sound nearby can make rice jump on a drum skin, make a window rattle or be felt in a balloon held in the hands.
understand: It works in both directions: vibrations make sound, and sound makes vibrations.
do: Show a sound making something vibrate, and describe what was seen or felt.

key_questions.note: My judgement. A VCAA elaboration has students find patterns between the volume of a sound and the strength of the vibrations that produced it.
key_questions.question: How can we make a sound louder or quieter?
know: Volume is how loud or quiet a sound is.
A stronger action (a harder hit, a bigger pluck, a harder blow) makes a bigger vibration.
understand: Bigger vibrations make louder sounds and smaller vibrations make quieter sounds.
do: Make the same sound louder and quieter on purpose, and say what was changed.

key_questions.note: My judgement. A VCAA elaboration has students find patterns between the pitch of a sound and features of the object that produced it. Keeping pitch apart from volume answers a misconception the research summaries report.
key_questions.question: How can we make a sound higher or lower?
know: Pitch is how high or low a sound is.
Short, small, thin or tight things usually make higher sounds. Long, big, thick or loose things usually make lower sounds.
understand: Pitch depends on the thing that is vibrating, not on how hard it is hit.
A sound can be high and quiet, or low and loud. Pitch and volume change separately.
do: Put a set of sounds in order from lowest to highest and describe the pattern, for example the longer the ruler, the lower the sound.
Change the pitch of a sound without changing its volume, and the volume without changing the pitch.

vocabulary.note: The choice of words and tiers is my judgement. Words marked as in the description were checked against the official wording. Loudness and pitch are named as target vocabulary in a VCAA elaboration. High, low, soft and volume all have other everyday meanings, so they need explicit teaching.

academic.meaning: Something that happens the same way again and again.
To look for what is the same and what is different.

science.meaning: To shake back and forth very quickly.
How high or low a sound is.
How loud or quiet a sound is.
The thing a sound comes from.
The achievement standard's term. At this level: sound can make things move.
A sound that bounces back so it is heard again.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the IOPSpark review and the RESPeCT Grade 1 list. I did not read the studies themselves. Eshach and Schwartz worked with middle school students. The IOPSpark review says younger students hold the idea too.
misconceptions.idea: Sound is a kind of stuff that lives inside the instrument or object. Hitting or blowing it lets the sound out.
misconceptions.science: Nothing is stored inside. The object vibrates, and the vibration is the start of the sound.
misconceptions.respond: Ask where the sound is before the drum is hit. Then touch a ringing triangle to stop it and ask where the sound went.
research: Operation Physics, American Institute of Physics (no date)

misconceptions.note: Checked against the IOPSpark review and the Research-2-Practice summary, which both report that pupils use vibration only where it can be seen and fall back on the action (you hit it hard) elsewhere. I did not read Asoko, Leach and Scott.
misconceptions.idea: Only things you can see shaking make sound by vibrating. A clap, a bang or a voice is made by the hitting or the person, not by a vibration.
misconceptions.science: Every sound comes from something vibrating. Often the vibration is too small or too fast to see.
misconceptions.respond: After the ruler and the elastic band, go to less obvious sounds: feel the throat while humming, touch a speaker, hold a balloon near a voice.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the IOPSpark review. The studies it names were with middle school students in Taiwan and Israel, so how common this is at ages 5 to 8 is not confirmed. I did not read the studies.
misconceptions.idea: It makes a sound because it is metal, or because it is hard, or because the string is tight.
misconceptions.science: The material changes what the sound is like, but the sound is made because the object vibrates.
misconceptions.respond: Ask the same question of two objects made of the same material, one ringing and one held still. What is different?

misconceptions.note: The Research-2-Practice lesson plan and the RESPeCT Grade 1 list both name this as a common idea in primary school. The studies named by IOPSpark were with secondary and university students. I did not read them.
misconceptions.idea: High means loud and low means quiet. Pitch and volume are the same thing.
misconceptions.science: Pitch (high or low) and volume (loud or quiet) are separate. A sound can be high and quiet, or low and loud.
misconceptions.respond: Make four sounds on one instrument: high and loud, high and quiet, low and loud, low and quiet. Students sort them twice, once by pitch and once by volume.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the Research-2-Practice summary (citing Allen, 2014) and the RESPeCT Grade 1 list. I did not read Allen. This is about how sound travels, which is beyond the description, but it comes up as soon as students talk about hearing.
misconceptions.idea: A sound is only in the ears of the person who hears it, or it goes only to that person.
misconceptions.science: Sound spreads out from its source in all directions, whether or not anyone is there to hear it.
misconceptions.respond: Stand students in a ring around one sound source and ask who can hear it. Then ask whether it made a sound for the students facing away.
research: Operation Physics, American Institute of Physics (no date)

misconceptions.note: Checked against the Research-2-Practice summary (citing Chang et al., 2007 and Driver et al., 1994) and the IOPSpark review. I did not read the studies. This matters for the VCAA earmuffs elaboration.
misconceptions.idea: Sound gets through things only by leaking through gaps and holes. A solid wall or cover simply blocks it.
misconceptions.science: Sound can pass through solid materials by making them vibrate. Soft, thick materials soak up more of the vibration, so less sound gets through.
misconceptions.respond: Put an ear to the desk while a partner taps the far end. Then compare how well different materials muffle a ticking timer.

misconceptions.note: My judgement. I found no study for it. It is the first half of the description, which most sound teaching skips.
misconceptions.idea: Vibrating things make sound, but a sound cannot make something else move.
misconceptions.science: Sound can make materials vibrate. That is how rice jumps on a drum skin near a loud clap.
misconceptions.respond: Predict first, then clap or bang a tray next to rice on a stretched skin without touching it.

inquiry.note: The code and its wording were checked in the curriculum. None of its elaborations mention sound, so the link is my judgement.
inquiry.how: Students predict before each test: will the longer ruler sound higher or lower? Will the rice move if nobody touches the drum?

inquiry.note: Two VCAA elaborations for this code use sound: suggesting materials and equipment to test predictions and measure the loudness of sounds made by different objects, and following steps to construct a musical instrument.
inquiry.how: Students follow picture steps to build a simple instrument, and suggest what they would need to test which object makes the loudest sound.

inquiry.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code names clap-o-meter apps that measure sound volume and slow-motion video of a vibrating ruler. I have not checked which sound meter apps are on the school iPads.
inquiry.skill: Planning and conducting: observing and recording
inquiry.how: Students film a twanging ruler in slow motion on an iPad to see the vibration, and use a simple sound meter app to compare loud and quiet.

inquiry.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code has students find patterns in the sounds made by saucepan lids of different sizes or elastic bands of different thicknesses.
inquiry.how: Students order objects from lowest to highest sound in a provided table and describe the pattern (bigger lid, lower sound).

inquiry.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code has students compare their observations of sound with those of others and consider whether everyone senses sound in the same way.
inquiry.how: Pairs compare which sound each judged higher or louder, talk about why they might differ, and say what they want to find out next.

human_endeavour.note: The VCAA lists this as an elaboration of VC2S2U12 itself.
human_endeavour.hook: Echoes and echolocation: where echoes happen, and how dolphins, bats and some people with vision impairment use echoes to find objects around them.

human_endeavour.note: Both examples are VCAA elaborations for this code.
human_endeavour.hook: People use what they know about sound every day: managing sound at home so it does not disturb others (closing doors quietly, shoes off on wooden floors), and toys and digital tools that respond to sound or to a voice.

human_endeavour.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code lists sound recordings among the ways scientists make observations. The link to the lesson is my suggestion.
human_endeavour.hook: Scientists observe with their ears as well as their eyes. Some record sounds, such as bird or frog calls, so they can listen again and compare.

human_endeavour.note: There is no First Nations elaboration for sound at Foundation to Level 2. The only VCAA link is a Levels 9 and 10 elaboration (VC2S10U14) on how the choice of material affects the sound of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' traditional musical, hunting and communication instruments. Which instruments, and what is appropriate to share or handle, I did not check. Use a named Koorie source or the school's Koorie education contacts before teaching it.
human_endeavour.hook: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have long chosen materials for the sound they make, in instruments for music and for communication.

below.summary: There is no level below. Foundation to Level 2 is the first band of the Science curriculum, and Foundation has no separate content descriptions.

same.note: The code and its wording were checked in the curriculum. The link is my judgement.
same.label: Pushes and pulls
same.summary: Pushes and pulls change how objects move, and can be stronger or weaker. Striking, plucking and blowing are pushes and pulls, and a stronger one makes a louder sound.

same.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code covers the five sensory organs, including ears, and echolocation in bats.
same.label: Features and senses
same.summary: The external features of plants and animals and what they do. Ears are the feature that detects sound, and some animals rely on echoes.

same.note: The code and its wording were checked in the curriculum. No elaboration mentions sound, so the link is my judgement. It is the pairing in the hub's curriculum file and in the Sound Signals unit.
same.label: Properties of materials
same.summary: Design and Technologies: the properties of materials and components used in designs. The material chosen changes how a home-made instrument sounds.

same.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code has students assemble the containers, contents and joining materials for musical shakers and check they work.
same.label: Making designs safely
same.summary: Design and Technologies: using materials, components, tools and techniques to make designs safely. Making a shaker or box guitar is this description at work.

same.note: The code and its wording were checked in the curriculum. No Digital Technologies elaboration at this level mentions sound, so this is my judgement and a loose link. The Sound Signals unit lists this code.
same.label: Exploring digital systems
same.summary: Digital Technologies: exploring digital systems and their parts for a purpose. It fits when students record and play back sounds on an iPad, or trigger sounds with a Makey Makey.

above.summary: There is no content description about sound at Levels 3 and 4, or at Levels 7 and 8. After Level 2, sound comes back by name only at Levels 9 and 10, so this is the one planned chance in primary school to teach how sounds are made.

above.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code has students show electrical energy being transformed into heat, light and sound.
above.label: Electrical circuits
above.summary: Energy is transferred and transformed in electrical circuits. Sound appears as one thing electrical energy can become, for example in a buzzer.

above.note: The code and its wording were checked in the curriculum. The link is my judgement: the description does not mention sound.
above.label: Light
above.summary: How light is produced, travels and meets objects. Students who know how sound is made and blocked can compare it with light. The two are joined as waves at Levels 9 and 10.

above.note: The description names sound alongside movement and light.
above.label: Electricity to sound
above.summary: Design and Technologies: how electrical energy is transformed into movement, sound or light in a product or system.

above.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code explains how digital systems store audio as whole numbers for the amplitude of the sound wave.
above.label: Audio as numbers
above.summary: Digital Technologies: how digital systems represent text, images and audio as numbers. This is where recorded sound is explained.

above.note: VCAA elaborations for this code link the volume of a sound to the amplitude of its wave and pitch to frequency, model sound with slinky springs, and look at material choice in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' instruments.
above.label: Waves
above.summary: Wave and particle models of energy transfer, and the features of waves. Volume and pitch from Level 2 return as amplitude and frequency. The direct next step, seven or eight years later.

anchors.note: The twanged ruler is an example in a VCAA elaboration, and slow-motion video of it is in another. The lesson shape is my suggestion and has not been trialled.
anchors.title: The twanging ruler
anchors.phenomenon: A ruler held flat on the edge of a desk and flicked makes a sound, and the end can be seen blurring up and down. Slide more of it off the desk and the sound drops lower. Flick it harder and it gets louder, not higher.
anchors.students_do: Predict, then twang with a short, medium and long overhang and order the sounds from low to high. Then keep the length the same and flick gently and firmly. Film one twang in slow motion to see the vibration.
materials: A 30 cm ruler for each pair (plastic and wooden give different sounds)
anchors.shows: Vibrating materials make sound. The length of the vibrating part changes the pitch, and the strength of the action changes the volume.
anchors.caution: Change one thing at a time, length or strength, or pitch and volume will blur together. Hold the ruler down firmly near the desk edge.

anchors.note: My suggestion, not trialled. It is the half of the description that the ruler does not show: sound making a material vibrate. Balloons and baking paper are on the STEAM room inventory. Rice or salt and elastic bands are not listed.
anchors.title: Jumping rice and a buzzing balloon
anchors.phenomenon: Rice grains sitting on baking paper stretched over a cup jump when someone claps or bangs a tray beside them, with nothing touching the cup. A balloon held between the hands buzzes when a partner talks into it.
anchors.students_do: Predict whether the rice will move, then test a quiet clap and a loud bang from the same distance. Hold a balloon lightly and feel it while a partner hums low and high sounds against the other side.
materials: A paper or plastic cup with baking paper stretched over the top and held by an elastic band
A pinch of rice or salt
A metal tray or saucepan lid and a spoon to bang near it
A blown-up balloon for each pair
anchors.shows: Sound can make materials vibrate, and a louder sound makes a bigger vibration.
anchors.caution: Bang beside the cup, not over it, so breath or a bumped desk does not move the rice. Check for latex allergies before using balloons.

anchors.note: Elastic bands of different thicknesses and box guitars are examples in VCAA elaborations. The lesson shape is my suggestion and has not been trialled.
anchors.title: Elastic band box guitar
anchors.phenomenon: Elastic bands stretched around an open container each make a different note when plucked. Thick and loose bands sound low, thin and tight bands sound high.
anchors.students_do: Pluck each band and order them from lowest to highest in a table. Find the pattern, then pluck one band gently and firmly to change only the volume.
materials: An open container for each pair, such as a takeaway tub or tissue box
Three or four elastic bands of different thicknesses
anchors.shows: Different actions and different features of the object produce sounds of different pitch and volume, and there is a pattern to find.
anchors.caution: Bands can snap or be flicked. Set the rule that bands stay on the box.

pitfalls.note: The Research-2-Practice summary (citing Asoko et al., 1992 and Viennot, 2001) recommends giving pupils sound-making experiences in less obvious contexts as well as obvious ones, because they do not carry the vibration idea across by themselves.
pitfalls.pitfall: Using only sounds where the vibration is easy to see, such as strings, rulers and drums.
pitfalls.instead: Once the idea is in place, take it to sounds with no visible vibration (a voice, a clap, a whistle, a speaker) and ask each time what is vibrating.

pitfalls.note: My judgement, from the wording of the description and the achievement standard, which both start with what sound does to objects.
pitfalls.pitfall: Teaching only that vibrations make sound, and leaving out that sound makes materials vibrate.
pitfalls.instead: Plan one experience where students see or feel a sound moving something without touching it.

pitfalls.note: My judgement, from comparing this description with VC2S10U14 in the curriculum.
pitfalls.pitfall: Explaining sound with waves, particles or the inside of the ear.
pitfalls.instead: Stay with what students can see, feel and hear: something vibrates, and the sound changes when the vibration changes. Waves wait until Levels 9 and 10 (VC2S10U14).

pitfalls.note: My judgement about the cause. That students mix up pitch and volume is reported in the sources.
pitfalls.pitfall: Letting the words blur. High and low are used for volume in everyday talk (turn it up, turn it down), soft can mean quiet or squashy, and volume has a different meaning in Maths.
pitfalls.instead: Fix the pairs and keep to them: loud and quiet for volume, high and low for pitch. Show both words with a gesture or picture every time.

pitfalls.note: My judgement, not based on a source.
pitfalls.pitfall: Twenty-five instruments played at once. Nobody can hear a pattern, and it is hard on students who are sensitive to noise.
pitfalls.instead: Set a silence signal first, test in turns or in pairs, and keep loud tests short. Offer a quieter spot or ear defenders to any student who needs them.

unverified: I could not read the original research studies. Each verified misconception rests on a published summary that I read and that names the studies. Several of those studies were with students older than Years 1 and 2 (the notes say which), so how common each idea is at ages 5 to 8 is not confirmed.
The last misconception (that sound cannot make things move) is my judgement. I found no study for it.

There is no First Nations elaboration for sound at Foundation to Level 2. The First Nations hook leans on a Levels 9 and 10 elaboration and names no instrument or community. I did not find or check a Koorie source.
None of the three anchor experiences has been trialled. Rice or salt and elastic bands are not on the STEAM room inventory, and I did not check which sound meter apps are on the iPads.

The lines on the map are my judgement about how the descriptions connect. The VCAA does not publish links between content descriptions. The Digital Technologies link at Foundation to Level 2 is a loose one with no elaboration behind it.
